title: the sounds
hook: a name read wrong off a list, and a grammar that measures a vowel by how long it's held
tomorrow: how can a puff of air on your palm change a whole word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds you can feel: the anusvara, one dot that hums in the shape of the next letter. Today, sounds changed by nothing but time.

Roll call on the first day of anything. A name gets read off the list, and the vowels come out squashed, or stretched in the wrong places. Some people correct it every time. Some give up after a week and answer to the wrong name for years. It can feel small and still sting. Sanskrit takes that sting seriously, because in Sanskrit, how long a vowel is held can change the word.
screen: `ROLL CALL.` → `THE VOWELS COME OUT WRONG.` → `SMALL, AND IT STILL STINGS.`

segments.voice: Panini measures vowels by time. The short one, hrasva. The long one, dirgha, held for longer. And an extra-long one, pluta, which he names for calling out to someone far away: the vowel stretches to cross the distance. Devanagari lets the eye see it. The short a lives inside every consonant, with no mark at all. The long a gets its own upright stroke after the letter. Now two words that look almost alike. Mata, both vowels short, is a thought, an opinion. Mata with both vowels long is mother. Same consonants. Only the holding changed. Names work the same way. Rama begins long and ends short: RAH-muh, not ruh-MAH. Priya, which means dear, has a short i and a long a at the end. So when someone at roll call stretches the wrong vowel, in Sanskrit's terms they're saying a slightly different word. Getting a name's length right is a small way of saying: I heard you. And a reader's first job with a verse is the same patience: give each long vowel its full time, and keep the short ones light.
screen: `SHORT, LONG, AND PLUTA.` · `THE LONG A GETS A STROKE.` · `A THOUGHT, OR MOTHER.` · `A NAME HAS ITS LENGTHS TOO.` · then, large: `HOLD THE LONG ONES LONG.`

segments.voice: Say Rama softly a few times, letting the first vowel take its full length and the last stay light. Then say one name you love, slowly, giving every vowel exactly the time it asks for. Let the last one fade, and rest with the breath.
The sounds: today, measured by the clock. Short, long, and the extra-long call across a distance.
Your line: the sounds. A long vowel is held, and a short one stays light, in a verse and in a name. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Sanskrit students learn vowel length by ear, repeating after a teacher, and chanters of the Vedas and the Gita take care to give long vowels their full time.
